items: Identify Destruction Zones: Walk through your home and write down every surface your kitten has scratched, climbed, or chewed without interpreting the behavior—just list what you observe.
Remove High-Risk Items: Move fragile objects, valuables, and toxic houseplants out of your kitten's reach or into a closed room to eliminate immediate destruction opportunities.
Cover and Secure Cords: Bundle all electrical cords and cover them with cord protectors to prevent chewing hazards and protect your electronics from damage.
Use Timeout Spaces: When feeling overwhelmed, place your kitten in a safe room with food, water, and a litter box while you calm yourself down.
Place Vertical Sisal Posts: Install tall sisal scratching posts directly next to couch corners and walls where your kitten already scratches to provide an appropriate alternative.
Add Horizontal Cardboard Scratcher: Position cardboard scratchers in areas where your kitten performs bunny-kicks and play to redirect that energy toward appropriate surfaces.
Position Climbing Alternatives: Set up cat trees or shelves near destroyed vertical spaces like curtains to give your kitten proper climbing outlets.
Match Alternatives to Each Zone: Place scratching and climbing options directly adjacent to the exact spots your kitten is destroying, never across the room.
Schedule Three Play Sessions: Plan two to three 15-20 minute interactive wand toy sessions daily to properly tire your kitten before chaos escalates.
Use Wand Toys for Real Play: Engage your kitten with wand toys that simulate prey movement rather than letting them entertain themselves with floor toys.
End Sessions With Food: Follow each play session with a meal so your kitten associates tiredness with satisfaction and naturally falls asleep afterward.
Reframe Destruction as Unmet Need: Remind yourself that scratching, climbing, and chewing are your kitten's biological drives, not personal attacks on your home.
